Solid-state RF is real and gives continuous power control that helps gentle thawing, though GaN amplifiers at this power are currently costly, not cheaper.
Mode stirrers are already common in microwaves and improve evenness, but this is a modest substitution that also has questionable cost savings.
Reflected-power sensing for endpoint detection is plausible and useful, but it ends thawing rather than speeding it, and it adds parts instead of being cheaper.
Package RFID tags need ecosystem adoption, and UHF tags in a microwave cavity risk damage, so it doesn't speed thawing.
Steering energy to the ice with patch antennas is interesting, but the high-power coupling, arcing and a magnetron-fed patch array make it technically doubtful.
Reflected-power sensing of melt state is plausible and useful for butter prep, though the signal is subtle and varies with load, and it is only a partial substitute for a timer.
A paddle driven through the floor would be hard to make safe in a microwave and the magnetic coupling is hand-wavy, but it does combine melting and mixing.
Thermochromic indicators are cheap and feasible, but they show surface temperature only and are a modest, familiar idea.
Passive RFID temperature tags read inside a microwave cavity face heavy interference and heating problems, though the remote alert is useful.
Tagged cups that set power automatically are practical and simplify prep, though the cup alone does not account for varying quantities.
Mode stirrers are an established technology, but removing the turntable does eliminate the glass plate and roller ring to clean, though the ceiling vane itself can get splattered.
A flush door without mesh holes is easier to wipe, but transparent conductive coatings at microwave-grade shielding are hard, and the camera adds complexity and a lens that gets dirty.
Sealed touch panels are common and easy to wipe, but they mainly affect the exterior and not the cavity, which is where cleaning matters most.
A removable PPS liner directly protects the cavity walls and is washable, and it is plausible, though liners may warp or absorb odors and some soil will get behind them.
Heat pipes with a membrane vent are inventive but impractical for a magnetron's heat load, and the link to cavity cleanliness is only indirect.
A picture drum with cam presets directly removes the need to read numbers and is cheap and buildable, though similar icon-based controls already exist.
Push-to-open doors are already common and only simplify door opening, a minor part of operation.
Drawer microwaves exist and are intuitive to load, but they are costly and do nothing to simplify the controls.
Auto-stop on steam with a single start button removes time setting, though sensor cooking already exists in higher-end ovens and is less reliable for dry foods.
Dish caps that set the oven mechanically are a radical idea that removes the panel, but they require proprietary containers and many variants.
Reflected-power sensing is a clever, cheap reuse of existing hardware, but mapping load signature to doneness across varied foods is difficult and unreliable.

Sub-wavelength mesh passes LWIR in principle, but the glass door is opaque to LWIR, so it needs a germanium or similar window, and the sensor needs shielding from RF; still, it directly shows temperature.
Outcome-based dial is a good concept but is vague about the sensing method and resembles existing sensor-cook features.
VOC sensing with multi-sense alerts is concrete and accessible, though MOX sensors are noisy and doneness correlation is imprecise.
A glanceable color ring is simple and readable, but thermochromic ink on a turntable underside is a weak proxy for food temperature and is not durable.
IR temperature sensing is highly relevant and plausible, though some microwaves already offer similar sensors, and it adds a part rather than simplifying.
A passive ready indicator is clever, but the underside color is hard to see, the film may not survive in the microwave, and the vessel temperature differs from the milk's.
A steam whistle cue is simple and tied to the drink, but microwaves are closed cavities, so the vent steam is unreliable and the cue comes late.
Nucleation sites directly address superheating eruptions in milk, though porous ceramic is hard to clean, can absorb milk, and has to stay microwave transparent.
A PTC plate can warm milk safely and cheaply, but it is no longer a microwave, and heating is slow, so it's a radical substitution that sacrifices speed.
Solid-state RF is real and could improve efficiency and control, though current GaN cost and efficiency (~50-60%) are only comparable to magnetrons, so the gain is modest.
Phased-array steering is plausible with solid-state RF and removes the turntable motor, but the energy saved is small and the idea depends on idea 1.
Microwave waste heat is low-grade and small, so the recovery loop adds cost and complexity for tiny savings, and magnetron cooling needs are real.
Sensor-based doneness detection already exists in commercial microwaves, but it does cut wasted cooking energy and is highly feasible.
Load shifting adds battery conversion losses and cost, and does not reduce total energy use; the cooking bursts are too short for the benefit to be significant.
Solid-state RF is real, but the claim that tuning frequency spares fats and vitamins is weak, and the tie to healthy diet is indirect.
Steam cooking directly serves nutrient retention and low fat and is feasible, though steam microwaves already exist and ultrasonic mist is cool rather than true steam.
Sensing doneness to prevent overcooking helps nutrients modestly, and similar sensors already exist, but in-cavity capacitive sensing is difficult.
Susceptor browning plates are proven and cut added fat, but they are not novel.
Frequency sweeping for even heating is plausible and removes moving parts, but its link to nutrition is tenuous.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and removes kV hazards, though cost and efficiency are still hurdles for consumer units.
Removing the mesh window cuts a leak path and is feasible, but a camera in a hot, humid, RF-filled cavity is challenging and the radiation gain is modest.
Capacitive sensing adds a useful redundant safeguard, but it is unreliable inside a metal cavity and does not replace interlocks, which are required.
Cool-touch shells address burns, but a vacuum skin traps heat from the magnetron and electronics, and the cabinet still needs cooling.
Removing exposed mains is a clever idea, but a kW-class 48 V inductive link is inefficient and bulky, and the mains cord is not the main hazard.
Real but tiny savings, since modern microwaves use LEDs or 20-25 W bulbs only briefly; camera adds cost and complexity, and the 'substitute' is cheap-ish but not simpler.
Inverter microwaves already exist, so it is feasible and efficient but not radical; the GaN/SiC claim is somewhat overreaching at 20-40 kHz.
Needs multiple solid-state sources and is costly, and the turntable motor uses negligible energy; targeted heating is the real efficiency benefit.
Waveguide losses are already small, so the gain is marginal; the probe feed is plausible but has arcing and power-handling risks.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and offers controllability and efficiency gains, though it is currently expensive and the cathode filament loss is small.
Solid-state RF is real and radical, but magnetron warm-up is only about a second, so the time saving is small and GaN cost is high.
Auto-stop saves re-runs and guesswork, but sensing a done-point from magnetron current is unreliable across foods and similar sensors already exist.
A load cell with lookup-table programs is cheap and easy and removes dial fiddling, but weight-based auto-cook is fairly obvious.
Phase-steered multi-feed cavities are plausible and have been researched, but they need coherent multi-source RF, which is costly, and the time saving is indirect.
Phone alerts are trivially feasible and already common in smart appliances, and they save attention rather than cooking time.
Solid-state RF is real and plausible, but magnetrons warm up in about a second, so the time savings are modest; its main benefits are even heating and fine power control.
Sensor-based auto-cook already exists in many microwaves, so it is not radical, but it clearly saves time and avoids guesswork and reheating.
Scan-to-cook tags are plausible and have been tried, and they depend on manufacturer adoption, but they remove programming effort.
Inverter supplies already ship in microwaves, and the claimed time savings are weak because the transformer was never a real delay.
A conveyor tunnel is radical and suits batch cooking, but it has RF leakage and size problems and is impractical for home kitchens.
Solid-state RF raises efficiency and control, and it is real technology, but cost and thermal limits at 700 W remain hurdles.
Beam steering is a bold idea, but the saved motor power is tiny and a phased array in a cavity is costly and complex, so it is not a cheaper substitute.
Sensor-based doneness cutoff is plausible and saves energy, but existing microwaves already offer similar sensing, so it is not very novel.
Coax feeding is simpler in principle, but the waveguide's losses are already small and it is hard to keep power handling and safe isolation.
LEDs cut lamp power, which is a minor part of total energy use, and the camera adds cost and its own consumption.
Solid-state RF is real and could improve efficiency through fine power control, but GaN cost and efficiency (~50-60%) are not yet clearly better than a magnetron, and it is not cheaper or simpler.
Persistent phosphor glow is too dim and fades quickly, and the lamp is a minor energy draw; coatings in a hot, greasy cavity are also impractical.
Fan-driven stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves, and the savings of a few watts from the turntable motor are marginal.
Reflection-based end-of-cycle detection avoids overcooking waste and is plausible, though inferring food state from reflection is imprecise; related sensors already exist.
Waste heat recovery is creative, but microwaves lose little heat and the recovered energy is minimal while the added cost and complexity are high.
A steered ultrasonic chime is a wild but plausible way to call the user back from anywhere, though it needs user tracking and room-wide reach, and it is not much of a substitution.
A tap-to-set NFC tag is feasible and cheap, but it only removes dial fiddling and does little to free the user from waiting by the oven.
Thermopile doneness sensing is practical and lets the user walk away trusting the result, though similar IR sensing already exists in ovens.

A wheeled, self-navigating microwave removes the need to walk to the appliance entirely and is radical, but it is costly and unsafe to move hot food around, and it is the opposite of a cheaper substitution.
A wearable haptic alert directly frees the user to roam and is very easy to build, but the idea is quite obvious and similar to existing smart appliance notifications.
A pictogram drum replacing the time and power knobs directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, though picture-based presets are not very radical.
A spring-loaded door that pops open at the end of the cycle is plausible and helpful, but it addresses only retrieval, not the operation of settings.
Handle light and vibration cues make status clear without a timer to read, but they do little to simplify input.
A one-button start with a humidity-based auto-stop removes setting time, but sensor-cooking already exists and accuracy varies across foods.
Reading cooking programs from NFC tags on packaging is a genuinely zero-setup concept, but it depends on food makers adopting the tags and on an ecosystem that does not exist.
Acoustic levitation of food-sized, heavy objects is not physically plausible, and the link to nutrient retention is indirect.
Sensor-based doneness detection is plausible and already partly exists, and it supports nutrient preservation, though the 'peak nutrient' endpoint is hard to define.
Solid-state RF is real and gives precise power control, but it is expensive and the nutrient benefit comes mainly from low-power control.
A steam-retaining vented vessel is highly feasible and directly serves nutrient retention and oil-free cooking, but it is largely an existing product.
Superheated steam crisping cuts the need for added fat and exists in steam ovens, but adding it to a microwave raises cost and complexity.

Removing the kV supply directly eliminates the shock hazard and the stored charge, and solid-state RF is real technology, but cost at 700 W and the 'substitute with something cheaper' constraint are weak points.
A transparent conductive door is plausible in principle, but ITO heating and RF leakage at the edges make it hard, and the safety gain over the existing mesh is modest.
IR thermal mapping to prevent superheating and burns is practical and cheap, though it only addresses burns and the title does not match the content.
A cool outer skin and no vents reduce burns and probing hazards, but a sealed shell with passive cooling of the magnetron is thermally difficult and aerogel adds cost.
mmWave presence sensing is novel and fast, but replacing mechanical interlocks is risky since they are fail-safe, and radar cannot reliably sense through the metal cavity.
Cool ultrasonic mist does not make 100 C steam without a heater, so the concept is muddled, but replacing the magnetron with steam cooking is radical and clearly serves the healthy-diet need.
Sensor-based doneness detection already exists in some microwaves, so it is plausible but incremental, and it only indirectly protects nutrients.
Mode stirrers are standard in many microwaves and the idea has only a weak link to nutrient retention.
A drip rack that drains fat is simple and works, and it directly lowers fat, though it is not very radical.
Returning condensate to the food is a nice idea, but removing the cooling fan is unrealistic because the magnetron needs cooling, and the nutrient gain is small.
IR endpoint sensing for butter state is useful and plausible, though the surface-temperature reading of a bowl and of the butter itself is imperfect, and the idea is not very radical.
A magnetic stirrer under the cavity floor is clever and serves mixing and melting, but it needs a non-metal floor, the coupling is weak for thick batter, and the magnet in the RF field is a concern.
Solid-state RF gives true low-power gentle melting and is real technology, but it is costly and is the opposite of a cheaper substitution.
A phone alert is easy and mildly useful for the prep step, but it is common in smart appliances and barely addresses baking a cake.
A camera behind a mesh lets the baker watch the bowl and replaces the lamp, but the heat and steam tolerance and the cost are questionable, and the benefit for cake is moderate.
Zero-input cooking is highly relevant, but inferring food type and a safe cook profile from low-power RF reflection is unreliable and the sensing is only loosely defined.
A simple, cheap substitution of the bell and release button that is easy to build, but it only addresses the end-of-cycle signal and not the operation itself.
Colour-coded status is intuitive and feasible, though it covers only feedback and not input, and light guides in the cavity must tolerate microwaves.
Placing food on the plate to load the program removes the interface entirely, but it depends on packaging adoption and on NFC tags surviving microwave fields, since metallic antennas may arc.
The drawer metaphor is familiar and radical, but sealing microwave leakage on a sliding cavity, the weight, and liquid spills make it hard, and it still needs time input.
Gas sensing of food aroma is plausible (already in some ovens) and directly signals doneness, though it is only loosely a cheaper substitute for the timer.
Using reflected power as a self-sensing signal is clever and cheap, but mapping it to doneness across varied foods is hard.
Passive thermochromic ink is simple and cheap, but it reads the tray temperature rather than the food's, and it is hard to see through the door; durability under washing is also a concern.
Rising tone is easy and a scent puff is feasible, but it only signals the timer's end, not true readiness, and the consumable cartridge adds cost, contradicting the substitute operator.
Listening to popping and bubbling is intuitive and works for popcorn, but it is noisy and unreliable for many foods, and the microphone has to survive the cavity environment.
Reflected-power sensing for thaw detection is plausible and directly useful, though it is known in solid-state RF research and adds parts rather than substituting cheaper ones.
Solid-state RF gives fine power control and even thawing, but GaN amplifiers at 50-150 W are currently costlier than magnetrons, so this is not a cheaper substitute.
Mode stirrers are a long-established technique, and removing the turntable can reduce uniformity for dense frozen blocks, though it is feasible and simplifies the design.
A water-bath thaw tray is an interesting buffer concept that evens out heating, but it is messy, adds sealing and hygiene issues, and diverts energy from the food.
A piezo alert is trivial and only peripherally helps defrost speed, so it is hardly radical.
Capacitive/permittivity sensing of thaw state is plausible and useful for auto-stop, though it adds sensing rather than speeding up defrost and substitutes a cam timer with a more complex system.
Susceptor plates are real and conduct heat, but heating from the bottom contact only modestly speeds thawing and risks cooking the surface; the substitution also does not obviously simplify things.
Lower-frequency deeper penetration is physically sound for thawing, but 915 MHz GaN arrays are large and costly, and the cavity must be much bigger, which makes this a poor cheaper substitute.
Phase control of a magnetron is poorly suited because the magnetron needs full heater and high-voltage drive, and it does not speed up defrosting.
Chilling the edges with cold air is an unusual idea, but it needs a refrigeration loop inside a microwave, which adds complexity and works against the aim of speed.
A tactile end-of-cycle thump is a novel idea, but a turntable-shaft cam can't be triggered at cycle end without extra actuation, and the vibration through the countertop would be weak.
A piezo that encodes time in pitch is easy to build and gives useful continuous audio feedback to blind users, though it is only a modest departure from existing beeps.
A click-detent dial that users set by touch and sound is highly usable for blind and elderly people, and mains counting is plausible, though the substitution is partly incidental.
A telecoil loop pad is a clever and feasible accessibility feature for hearing-aid users, but it targets hearing loss rather than vision and only helps those with telecoil-equipped aids.
Moulded tactile numerals are directly useful and cheap to make, but they are a common, well-known accessibility technique.
Spoken status directly serves blind and elderly users and is cheap and proven, though talking appliances already exist.
A tactile detent dial is highly accessible and simple, but it is a classic mechanical solution and not radical.
A large palm-press door release helps people with dexterity limits, but it mostly addresses motor rather than visual needs.
Auto-stop at target temperature removes the need to read a timer, but IR surface sensing is unreliable for microwave doneness.
A vibrating alert pad is a useful end-of-cycle signal for deaf-blind users, but it is a narrow add-on that does not replace much.
Load-cell weighing with a single category tap cuts settings substantially and is plausible, though it still needs a tap and mass is a crude proxy for cook time.
Tapping a packet is very intuitive, but it depends on packaging adoption and does nothing for food without tags, so it can't be the only way to operate.
A push-anywhere door is easy to use, but it only affects opening the door and leaves the cooking controls untouched; it's also a fairly small change.
A progress ring is clear and easy to build, but it only gives feedback and doesn't simplify input.
Hold-to-heat leaves nothing to learn and is simple to build, but holding a key for long periods is tiring and raises safety and ergonomics concerns.

Reflected-power sensing is a genuinely radical way to infer doneness, but load impedance varies widely between foods and is hard to map to doneness, and the coupler and detector are not cheaper than a timer.
Steam-plateau detection is plausible, and some commercial microwaves already use humidity sensors, so it directly serves the feedback need but is not very radical.
A BLE done-alert is cheap and feasible and reaches users away from the microwave, but it is a common smart-appliance idea and requires a paired device.

A thermochromic window is a creative passive indicator, but it only reads surface temperature, may not survive the microwave environment, and would not replace the lamp, which is needed to see inside.
Turntable motion is nearly free and accessible to deaf users, but it is a weak, easily missed signal from across the room and not very radical.
Highly relevant and very feasible, since talking tactile dials are proven, but the idea is not radical.
Interesting audio description of food state, but the thermal camera is costly rather than a cheaper substitute, and it does not help operate the controls; describing contents is also hard.
A feasible vibration alert, but it mainly serves hearing loss rather than visual impairment or the elderly need, and it is marginal.

A palm-plate sliding door helps dexterity and finding the controls, but a sliding microwave door with a latch and shielding is mechanically challenging and a capacitive plate is hard to locate without sight.
Tapping a package removes the need to read or set anything, but it depends on food-industry adoption of NFC tags and does not cover foods without tags.

IR sensing for melting butter to a target temperature directly addresses the prep task and is plausible, though IR sensors in microwaves already exist and the sensor replaces the timer rather than being a radical substitution.
A solid-state RF amplifier with continuous power control suits gentle melting and is real technology, but it costs more than a magnetron and works against the 'cheaper or simpler' substitution goal.
A passive colour cue is a charming idea, but a film on the door glass will not track butter temperature reliably, and the cavity is dark and shielded.
Susceptor sheets are real and do brown food, but they are well-known, consumable, and not a true replacement for the turntable motor, since the turntable's job is even heating.
Touchless door opening is practical for messy hands, but it is tangential to the cake-baking and butter-melting need, and it adds components rather than substituting cheaper ones.
Solid-state RF is real and offers fine power control, but it is costly and not substitute-cheaper, and it only loosely improves butter melting for cake prep.
IR sensing with feedback directly solves butter melting and is highly feasible, though similar sensor features already exist.
A PTC ceramic tray gives safe self-limiting melting, but it replaces microwave heating with conduction and the tray would be slow and a weak fit for a microwave.
A magnetic stirring bowl turns melting into mixing, which is useful for cake prep, but it is mechanically tricky inside a microwave cavity.
A connected recipe sequencer is easy to build but is common smart-appliance territory and only indirectly improves the melting itself.
Passive steam film is a creative lamp substitute, but condensation on the door is a weak and unreliable readiness signal, and film durability is doubtful.
Acoustic cue sensing is plausible, and the bidirectional piezo is elegant, but fan noise and food variety make detection unreliable.
Sensing magnetron load is clever and concrete, but absorbed power changes are subtle and inconsistent across foods, so inferring doneness is shaky.
IR thermopile sensing is real and already used in some ovens, so it is feasible and relevant but not radical, and it only reads surface temperature.
A thermochromic label gives direct, clear feedback and is feasible, but it only works with labelled packaged food and adds consumable cost.
Steam cleaning with a water dish is already common practice and works well, so it is highly feasible and relevant but not very novel.

A transparent conductive film door is a plausible, novel way to remove mesh holes, though ITO shielding at 2.45 GHz and its durability are real challenges, and the door is a minor cleaning pain point.
Magnetic levitation is radical, but it is complex and costly, and magnets near the magnetron and the heat make it hard; it only marginally improves cleaning.
A removable liner directly addresses cavity cleaning, but RF sealing, electrical contact and the waveguide opening make a dishwasher-safe liner hard to realise.
Sealed touch panels are already standard on many microwaves, so this is feasible and helps a little but is hardly new.

Capacitive hand sensing is a creative pre-emptive safeguard, but removing the mesh and the redundant mechanical interlocks is dangerous and unlikely to pass regulation, since RF shielding of the glass door is hard and capacitive sensing is unreliable.
Inverter microwaves already exist, but a GaN driver with no HV capacitor is a plausible shock reducer; the magnetron still needs about 4 kV, so the energy-storage claim is overstated.
Passive heat-pipe cooling removes the fan and hot exhaust, but magnetron heat loads are sizable and the safety benefit for the main hazards is marginal.
A thermopile array that predicts superheat targets a real scald hazard and is feasible, though it cannot see inside opaque containers and replacing the thermal cutouts would be unsafe.
A cool-touch composite shell with an RF barrier addresses burns, but a graphene polymer is unlikely to reliably contain microwave leakage and the shell has to withstand the cavity heat.
Highly relevant and very feasible, but talking appliances already exist so it is not radical.
Tactile stackable tokens are a creative, accessible input method, though losing tokens and the limited time granularity are drawbacks.
A haptic alert is feasible and useful, but it targets hearing more than the vision need, and a wristband adds an extra device to wear.
A scent alert is very novel, but it is slow, inconsistent, needs consumable cartridges, and is a weak fit for the vision/elderly need.

Spoken food-state description is a bold idea that serves visually impaired users, but a camera must survive heat, steam and splatter and the recognition has to be reliable, and it is not cheaper or simpler.
Directly frees the user from standing by the oven and is very practical, though wearable alerts are a fairly obvious idea.
Remote viewing of the cavity serves mobility, but it needs the user to watch a screen and it is not especially radical.
Voice control already exists and helps with setup rather than with waiting by the appliance, so it only partly addresses the need.
Very wild and creative, but a roaming magnetic puck in a microwave cavity is hard to build safely, and it only indirectly serves mobility.
Moving the appliance is novel, but kilowatt wireless power is impractical, and a movable microwave does little to remove the need to wait beside it.
Removes the turntable and gives a flat cavity, but solid-state RF arrays are costly and the cleaning benefit is indirect, so the idea does not follow the 'cheaper or simpler' substitute brief.
Steam cleaning is already common practice, but an automated cycle directly serves ease of cleaning and is plausible, though it adds a reservoir rather than substituting a part.
A TiO2 coating with UV-A LED replaces the lamp's role in a clever way, but photocatalysis is weak at the low UV power and ambient temperatures inside a microwave, so the benefit is doubtful.
A flush door panel is easy to wipe and feasible, but it only touches the exterior and leaves the interior, where cleaning matters most, untouched.
A removable dishwasher-safe liner substitutes a simple part for the hard-to-clean cavity and targets the need head-on, though sealing, fit and polymer durability under heat are real challenges.
Solid-state RF with continuous power is real and plausible (GaN at 2.45 GHz exists), improving defrost evenness, though the cost is high and the idea is not very wild.
Phase-controlled multi-feed field steering is a real solid-state-RF technique that reduces cold spots, but it requires multiple solid-state sources and is not a cheap substitute.
Reflected-power thaw detection is feasible and has been explored, and it helps with reliability and avoiding cooked edges more than with speed.
Removing the HV chain is mostly a safety and cost gain with little direct link to defrost speed, and it is dependent on solid-state RF at power.

A SiC lossy plate conducting heat from below is a concrete and unusual substitute for the turntable, but the plate would absorb microwaves and could overheat and cook the base, so the speed benefit is uncertain.
Solid-state RF replacing the magnetron is real and plausible, but cost at 700 W is high and magnetron warm-up is only about a second, so the speed benefit is marginal.
Phase-controlled multi-feed sweeping is a credible, concrete way to replace the turntable and improve evenness, but it depends on solid-state sources, so the cost is high.
Reflected-power sensing for doneness is plausible and saves guesswork, though accuracy across varied foods is hard and it does little for speed.
Package-coded tags give one-tap reheating and are technically easy, but they require food-industry adoption and are not truly a substitution of a part.
A flat single-plate cavity is radical and suits a single-portion reheat, but a 3 cm cavity struggles with field uniformity, food height and loading.
Picture cards with passive NFC tags are cheap and plausible, and they remove numeric settings, though users still have to find and insert the right card.
A single button with steam-based auto-finish removes all settings, and humidity-sensing cooking already exists in some ovens, so it is workable but not new.
A drawer is intuitive to open, but it only fixes the door release, leaves the timer and power controls untouched, and the RF choke at a drawer opening is harder to engineer.
Load cells set power automatically, but mass alone is a poor guide to what the food needs, and the user still has to set the time.
A camera that recognises the food plus one Yes button gives true zero-learning use, though recognition accuracy, cost and the mesh-sealed camera are real hurdles.
Solid-state RF is real and credible, but magnetron warm-up is only about a second, so the time savings are small; the main gains are control and lifespan.
Phased-array steering is plausible with solid-state sources and improves evenness, but it is costly and the cooking-time reduction is modest.
Package-coded programming exists in some forms and is easy to implement, and it removes setup steps, though it depends on packaging adoption.
Cooking several plates at once could save time, but splitting one source across stacked chambers cuts power per plate and is hard to engineer.
Adaptive impedance-matched thawing targets a real slow task and is technically feasible with solid-state RF, though the claim of minutes for thawing is optimistic.
Solid-state RF is real and gives true continuous low-power control that suits gentle butter melting, though cost is high and the substitution is not cheaper.
IR closed-loop melt endpoint directly solves scorching and timing, and is feasible, though sensor-equipped microwaves already exist.
Mode stirrers are well-known and proven, and the benefit for melting butter is moderate, so it is a low-novelty swap.
A susceptor cup suits small melts and easy cleanup, but susceptors heat by conduction and can overheat, and the idea is incremental.
A patch antenna and ceramic liner mostly address cleaning and cost, with only tangential benefit to baking a cake, and high-power patch launch is questionable.
Susceptor crisping is already in microwave packaging and some browning plates, but making it an oil-free sear is a plausible, concrete way to cut fat.
Sensor-based doneness detection already exists in microwaves, and the link to nutrient retention is indirect, though it is practical.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and is being commercialized, but the nutrient benefit of continuous power is modest and the parts are expensive.
Electronic field steering is plausible with solid-state sources, but it needs several of them and the nutrient link is indirect.
Microwave steaming directly protects water-soluble vitamins and is feasible, though steamer accessories already exist.
Auto-stop on temperature serves the need well, but magnetron current is a weak, unreliable proxy for liquid temperature, since it depends on load volume, line voltage and magnetron warm-up.
Magnetic stirring evens out heating and is plausible, but it adds parts, the stir bar must be microwave-safe, and it is not really a cheaper substitution.
Thermochromic ink is cheap and feasible and gives direct readiness feedback, though it only informs the user and does not control heating.
A steam whistle is a fun idea, but milk in a cup produces little pressurised steam and the vent geometry makes it unreliable.
Phase control on a magnetron transformer is problematic because the magnetron needs high-voltage conditions, so it is not truly continuous, and the idea is not very radical.
Solid-state RF is real and gives fine power control, but it is only indirectly tied to the milk need and is costly rather than cheaper or simpler.
IR sensing to stop at a target temperature directly solves overheating and is very feasible, though some microwaves already do it.
A magnetic stirrer prevents superheating and uneven heating, but a magnet and metal parts in a microwave raise safety and arcing concerns.
A single-mug resonant cavity is plausible and efficient, but single-mode tuning is sensitive to the load and so hard to get right.
Induction heating of a ferrous jug base is proven and safe, but it replaces the microwave altogether instead of substituting a part of it.

Radar presence sensing is novel, but replacing the interlocks entirely would be a regulatory and safety regression, since mechanical redundancy is required, and radar can't reliably detect a door gap or leakage.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and eliminates the kilovolt hazard, though it is costly, and the claim that it makes things safe after unplugging is overstated since the main risk is the capacitor.
Aerogel insulation helps with burns, but it is expensive, and a non-metallic wrapper conflicts with RF shielding, and it is not a cheaper substitution.
Camera-based metal detection is plausible and prevents arcing, but it adds cost, and it addresses fire more than the radiation, burn and shock hazards.
A fanless sealed heat-pipe cooling system removes the fan and vent hazards, but the magnetron's heat load is large and passive cooling at that scale is hard, and the hazard it removes is minor.
Solid-state RF is real and credible (already in some products), but it is costlier than a magnetron and its benefits for reheat speed are indirect.
Electronic sweep for even heating is plausible and tied to solid-state sources, but it is hard to calibrate and the turntable is already cheap, so the substitution is not clearly simpler.
Reflected-power sensing is a plausible way to cut overcooking, though it is less about speed and is unreliable on small or frozen loads.
Easy to build and genuinely convenient, but it depends on packaging adoption and isn't radical.
Pressurized steam reheating could be fast, but certification, safety and seal wear make it a hard sell for a household appliance, and it adds complexity rather than substituting something simpler.
Auto-stop via vision and IR sensing saves attention and prevents reheating, though camera-based doneness detection exists in some ovens and is hard inside a microwave cavity.
Solid-state RF is real and enables continuous power, but the time savings are modest and cost is high.
Phased multi-feed solid-state steering gives even heating without a turntable, but the time saving is indirect and it needs solid-state sources.
Dual drawers allow parallel use, which helps in batch cooking, but it does not speed single-meal cooking, and it adds components rather than substituting cheaper ones.
Magnetrons already start in about a second, so the claimed warm-up saving is negligible, though inverter supplies are real.
Humidity/VOC sensing for readiness is plausible (some microwaves already use humidity sensors) and directly gives food-state feedback, though the lamp substitution is only loosely tied.
Acoustic doneness detection is creative but unreliable, and a microphone in a microwave cavity with a sub-$0.30 classifier is unrealistic.
Outcome-based dial with sensor feedback is feasible but resembles existing sensor-cook modes and is vague on the feedback mechanism.
A clear ITO shield improves visual feedback, but ITO attenuation at microwave frequencies and durability under heat are questionable, and it only helps while the user is watching.
Phone alerts are easy and useful for remote notification but are a common connected-appliance idea, and the food state source is unspecified.
Offline voice control with spoken readback directly serves visually impaired and elderly users and is feasible, though voice-controlled appliances are already familiar.
A vibrating turntable is a creative tactile alert, but the existing motor can't easily spin an offset weight and the cue only helps if the user is touching the plate or the appliance.
Narrating food state is useful and imaginative, but a thermal camera in a microwave cavity faces harsh conditions and unreliable classification, and it adds cost rather than cutting it.
Scent as an end-of-cycle cue is very novel, but cartridges are consumable, release timing is hard to control, and it fails for users with a poor sense of smell, which is common among the elderly.
A wide palm-plate latch is simple, cheap, and makes the door easy to open for arthritic or blind users, although it is more of an incremental change.
Tap-to-cook via NFC removes dials, but requires tagged plates or packaging, which limits usefulness with ordinary food.
Weighing is feasible and removes the timer, but mass alone is a poor predictor of cook time and the turntable is awkward to build.
Humidity-based auto-stop is plausible, proven in sensor-cook microwaves, and strongly removes the need to guess a time.
A drawer is a radical form change, but it does little for operation learning and has serious microwave leakage and sealing challenges.
Offline keyword spotting is feasible, but it only sets power level and voice commands are already common, so the gain is modest.
Package-encoded cook instructions remove all operation, though it needs industry adoption and NFC inside a metal cavity is tricky.
Close-to-start is simple and feasible, but unintended starts (e.g. empty oven) and a default cycle limit usefulness and raise safety concerns.
A tactile end-of-cook signal is feasible but addresses notification rather than operation simplicity, so relevance to no learning curve is weak.
Closed-loop IR sensing removes time and power decisions, though surface-only readings are imprecise and similar sensors already exist.
Mode stirrers are proven and eliminate the tray, but they only marginally reduce operating complexity and are not radical.
Directly solves overheating or underheating with closed-loop IR sensing, but IR sensing in microwaves is already known and the surface reading can be misleading.

A passive readiness cue is cheap, but a film on the window is likely to be hard to make work, since it must be shielded for microwaves, tolerate heat, and read the drink's temperature rather than the window's.
Magnetic stirring is clever and addresses superheating, but it needs a special mug and bar, and the stir bar and magnet drive inside a microwave cavity creates arcing and metal risks.
Solid-state RF is a real, radical direction that gives precise power control, but it is costly and only loosely tied to the milk need, and it doesn't truly substitute for something cheaper.
A phone alert is feasible and convenient, but it is a notification gimmick, adds cost, and does not improve the heating itself; a tag in the mug is also awkward inside a microwave.
Placing food sets the program automatically, which removes the learning curve, but it depends on tagged packaging and the ring antenna sits near the microwave field.
Simple and very feasible, but it only fixes door opening, a minor part of operation, and pop-open doors already exist.
It would be zero-input if it worked, but impedance sensing for food type and mass is unreliable and unsafe to rely on for cook times.
Icon-based selection is intuitive and cheap to build, though it is an incremental change from a knob and still needs a timer.
A steam flag is a quirky replacement for a timer, but it does not simplify setting the cook and is unreliable for many foods.
Susceptor trays are real and would brown the cake base, though a metal-film disc replacing the glass tray raises arcing and durability concerns.
Solid-state RF is real and gives true continuous low power for gentle melting, but it is not cheaper and the 35-40°C dial claim is optimistic.
An IR sensor that stops at a target state is plausible and fits butter melting, though it only reads the surface temperature.
A feasible wristband alert, but it is only loosely tied to baking and adds cost rather than simplifying.
Thermochromic film on the door is imaginative but cannot show the cake's temperature, and removing the lamp hurts visibility.
Practical and cheap alert that frees the user to roam, though wearable alerts are fairly obvious and only partly radical.
Remote start and control is already common in smart microwaves, and it does not solve the need to load or unload food, but it serves mobility well.
Remote monitoring helps users stay away, but a camera in a microwave cavity is hard to make work and the idea does not substitute for the need to attend.
A motorized door is feasible, but it addresses only a minor part of standing by the appliance and has safety and usefulness limits.
A wild self-driving oven strongly serves mobility and is radical, but carrying hot, liquid-filled food on wheels is impractical, costly and unsafe, and it does not simplify the product.
Practical and cheap, directly lets users leave the kitchen, but wearable and smart-appliance alerts are fairly obvious.
Remote start does little for not standing by during cooking, and food must be loaded at the oven anyway, so relevance is weak.
Auto-stop gives confidence to walk away, but passive probes inside a microwave field are technically doubtful and it doesn't alert the user.
Wild and memorable delivery concept, but hot-food robots, navigation and safety make it impractical and arguably not a simpler substitute.
Portable battery microwave frees location, but power demands of hundreds of watts of RF from batteries make it hard, and it still needs attending less clearly.

Spoken food-state description is a creative substitute for the lamp and window, though a camera in a microwave cavity and reliable food recognition are hard, and the narration is only tangential to operating the controls.

A single tactile button with haptic and spoken confirmation directly removes small-print and fine-motor barriers and is easy to build, though press counting may burden users with cognitive impairment.
Auto-stop by vapour sensing removes timer setting, but sensor reliability across foods is questionable and some sensor-based microwaves already exist.
A drawer helps weak grip and reach, but a microwave drawer with a sliding RF seal is difficult, and it does little for visual impairment.
A haptic end-of-cycle alert is feasible and helpful, but it mainly serves hearing loss and addresses only the alert, not operating the microwave.
Solid-state RF is real and efficient, with per-cell modulation matching load, though cost is high and it is not very novel, and the 'substitute cheaper' angle is weak.
Removes the turntable motor, but the motor's energy use is tiny, so efficiency gains are marginal and it depends on a solid-state array.
Ending cooking at the true done-point saves energy, but sensor-based cooking already exists and in-band permittivity sensing is hard.
Recovering magnetron waste heat is creative, but the heat is low-grade, the loop adds complexity, and the benefit is small for short cook times.
Vacuum insulation is a wild idea, but microwave cavities lose little heat in short cooks, and the cost and RF-containment challenges are high.
Thermochromic mug is plausible and useful as a done-signal, but it only indicates temperature, doesn't heat, and the surface temperature lags the milk's.
Induction heating of milk is proven technology, though it effectively replaces the microwave rather than substituting a part, and it isn't very novel.
A magnetic stirrer is workable and reduces superheating, but a stir bar inside the cavity is awkward and clashes with microwave fields.
A smaller cavity is sensible and feasible, but it is a modest resizing, not a radical idea, and the specifics are thin.
A Curie-point self-limiting sleeve is clever for auto-cutoff, but ferrite susceptors in a microwave heat the vessel rather than the milk evenly, and a 65 C Curie point is hard to engineer.
Auto-loading settings from the pack eliminates all learning, but it needs industry-wide packaging adoption, and NFC readers and tags near a magnetron raise heating and arcing concerns.
A pictogram dial with a mechanical cam is simple and very feasible and cuts down on reading settings, but it is a modest rethink of existing dial microwaves.
A spring pop-open door removes the need to find the release, but it does nothing for setting up the cook and it could open unexpectedly.
An electrochromic progress window is novel, but it is hard to make work with the mesh and microwaves, it only shows status, and it does not simplify operation.
A single press-to-add-time button is very intuitive and cheap, and a mechanical ratchet substitutes well for electronics, though it is similar to existing quick-start buttons.
Practical and cheap wearable alert that replaces the bell, though wearable notifications are already common and it only frees the user from waiting rather than from retrieving.
A wild and memorable idea that brings the alert to the user, but a SLAM robot is costly and complex, not a cheaper or simpler substitute.
Remote start and tracking from a pocket puck is plausible and serves mobility, but remote starting with food inside raises safety questions and the puck is similar to a phone app.
Very radical, but an inductively driven glass tray that rolls out and delivers food is physically implausible and unsafe with hot food and liquids.
Routing the chime through existing speakers and push notifications is feasible and uses existing infrastructure, but it is an obvious idea and could be disruptive in shared spaces.
Highly relevant and very feasible, but talking appliances already exist so it is not radical.
Creative sound-based doneness sensing helps blind users, but reliable classification in a noisy, RF-filled cavity is hard.
A drawer helps mobility, but RF sealing, hot spills and the cost of sliding mechanisms are real problems, and it does little for visual impairment.
Touch-free opening helps weak grip, though accidental triggering and visually impaired discoverability are concerns, and it adds cost.
A practical tactile overlay directly serves visually impaired users and is cheap, but it is a well-known approach.
Solid-state RF with frequency sweeping and 915 MHz penetration directly targets uneven thawing and is physically plausible, though costly and not really a cheaper substitution.
Weight-based auto defrost already exists in the market; it improves convenience but doesn't make thawing faster.
Susceptor plate adds conductive heating from below and is plausible, but the heat transfer into the frozen block is limited and it could cause local cooking.
Cooling the surface while microwaves thaw the core is clever, but a Peltier plate inside a microwave cavity is hard and cooling the food works against speed.
Inverter-based continuous power exists in inverter microwaves; it helps gentle thawing but doesn't speed it up.

Solid-state RF is a real, emerging technology and a true substitute for the magnetron; the time savings are modest, since magnetron warm-up is only a second or two, but power control and efficiency do improve.
Phased-array beam steering is plausible and gives more even heating, but it saves less time than claimed, since turntable rotation doesn't add to cook time.
Camera-based auto-cook already exists in commercial products and cuts guesswork and reheats, but it is incremental rather than radical.
Easy to build, but the time savings are marginal, and an auto-open door and a phone view are gimmicks that don't speed up cooking.
A conveyor tunnel for batch throughput is radical and does serve time savings for groups, but it is bulky, needs RF shielding at the openings, and doesn't fit a home kitchen.
Solid-state RF is real and substitutes the magnetron cleanly, but it does not truly speed up reheating since magnetrons already deliver full power quickly; its benefits are mainly control and safety.
Reflected-power sensing is plausible and saves guesswork, but detecting a 'target temperature' from reflection is unreliable and the phone alert adds little speed.
A conveyor tunnel is radical and industrial microwaves exist, but it is impractical for households in size, cost and leakage control, and it likely heats slower per plate.
Easy to build and handy with full hands, but it saves only seconds and does not touch the reheating speed itself.
SiC susceptors are real and give browning, though a fixed plate gives uneven RF heating without a turntable and does not clearly cut reheating time.
Practical and directly frees the user from standing by, but wearable alerts are a fairly common concept and it substitutes little.
Smart packaging with NFC tags is plausible and removes setup effort, but it only indirectly addresses mobility since the microwave still needs to be checked at the end.
Truly radical and brings the appliance to the user, but a self-driving microwave carrying hot food raises serious safety and cost concerns, and it is not a cheaper substitution.
Using existing office lighting as a notification channel is creative and serves the need, though it requires integration with building systems and is less personal in shared offices.
A camera in place of the lamp enables remote monitoring, but heat, steam and splatter are issues, and checking the food remotely does not tell the user when it is done as directly as an alert would.
Solid-state RF is real and plausible, but it is only loosely tied to butter melting and the slower heating is a drawback for this need.
IR closed-loop melt-point control directly prevents scorching and removes guesswork, and is technically plausible, though IR sees only the surface and some microwave ovens already have sensors.
A conductive plate would even out heating, but it is labelled induction while described as conduction, and a metal-clad base conflicts with the microwave cavity.
A thermopile array camera is cheap and workable and gives remote melt monitoring, but it only observes and does not control the heating.
Susceptor sleeves are a known mechanism that plausibly helps fats melt, though the claim that fats barely absorb microwaves is overstated, and it substitutes an accessory rather than a part.

Replacing the HV capacitor/diode doubler with a high-frequency inverter is plausible and addresses shock risk, though the magnetron itself still needs ~4 kV and some stored energy, and inverter microwaves already exist.

RF-load sensing as a backup interlock is clever and substitutes for switches, but a loaded/unloaded state doesn't reliably indicate a slightly ajar door or leakage, so it works better as a redundant layer.
ITO film shielding is real but gives poor attenuation at 2.45 GHz at high power and can't remove the need for a seal at the door edges; heating and cost are issues.
Vacuum/aerogel insulation would reduce case burns and is technically viable, though it addresses only the exterior and adds cost, not a simplification; the hot food and door glass still remain.
A passive heat pipe replacing the fan removes a minor hazard but cooling a magnetron at ~1 kW without airflow is challenging, and the safety gain is marginal.
Solid-state RF is real and removes the kV rail and stored-charge hazard, though cost and efficiency are still hurdles; it is a strong substitution that directly serves the need.
A sealed door removes the mesh aperture, but the camera is a heat and steam challenge, and the leakage risk from mesh windows is already very low.
mmWave presence sensing adds a redundant safeguard beyond the interlocks and is plausible, but it risks false triggers and needs a fast RF kill, and it adds a part rather than substituting one.
Aerogel insulation and a rear exhaust are feasible and cut burn risk, but they are incremental and do nothing for radiation or shock.
Inductive power removes the cord and plug, but a microwave draws about 1.5 kW, so a pad would be inefficient, costly and still carry internal high voltage.
Practical and feasible wearable alert that frees the user from standing by, but a fairly incremental idea since smart appliance notifications already exist.
Wildly radical mobile microwave that delivers food, though a moving robot with a hot sealed cavity raises safety, cost and power issues.
Private ultrasonic alert is clever, but earbuds don't receive ultrasound and BLE would do the job far more simply.
NFC tag programming with phone countdown is realistic and concrete, though it addresses mobility only partly through remote monitoring.
Desk-embedded heating removes the trip entirely, but 700 W mid-range resonant transfer to a dish is inefficient, hard to shield and unsafe.
Solid-state RF is real and enables fine power control, but the health link (gentler temperature holding) is indirect and the cost is high.
Phased-array steering is plausible and gives even heating, but the nutrient benefit is modest and indirect.
An edible susceptor that browns food without oil directly cuts fat and is highly novel, but food-safety and a 200 °C edible carbon sheet are doubtful.
Camera and VOC sensing for doneness is plausible and prevents overcooking, but similar sensors already exist and it adds complexity rather than substituting something simpler.
Microwave steaming trays already exist and clearly preserve water-soluble vitamins, so it is highly feasible and relevant but not radical.
Removing the lamp saves only a few watts, and ambient light through a mesh-shielded door is too dim to see inside, so the substitution is weak and the benefit small.
Solid-state RF is a real, emerging technology that improves efficiency and control, though cost is high and the idea is already known.
Magnetron waste heat is modest and hard to couple into the cavity, and removing cooling risks overheating the magnetron, so the physics is questionable.
Sensor-based auto-stop genuinely avoids wasted energy, but it is established in existing microwaves and accurate dielectric sensing is hard.
Electronic field steering removes the turntable motor, but the motor's draw is tiny; the gain comes from more even heating and depends on solid-state sources.
Solid-state RF is real and enables precise, continuous power control, but the nutrient benefit is indirect, and it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.
Microwave steam cooking is already on the market, but it directly serves nutrient retention and fat-free cooking, and the idea is concrete.
Combo IR grill microwaves already exist, and the link to nutrient retention is weak, though it does reduce the need for frying oil.
Sensor cooking is already common, and it helps avoid overcooking, but the fat-reduction link is tenuous.
A fat-draining tray directly cuts fat and is plausible, but microwaves render little fat and the mechanism is simplistic.

Solid-state RF is real and enables fine power control and even heating, but it is costly and not clearly faster at defrosting, and it is more a substitution of the source than a defrost-specific innovation.
Susceptor plates are real and heat from below, but conduction into a large ice block is slow and surface-limited, so the claim of faster centre thawing is overstated.
Sensing the ice-to-water impedance change to detect thaw is plausible, and similar sensing has been explored; it makes defrosting easier and avoids cooking, though it does not speed it up.
Fan-driven mode stirrers are a known, cheap and feasible technology that improves uniformity, but it is not novel and not specific to defrosting.

A PCM thermal battery tray is unusual, but the salt hydrate melting point and the low heat it can deliver make it slow, and charging it by microwaves is questionable, so it is unlikely to defrost quickly.
Directly frees the user from waiting by the appliance and is very feasible, but wearable alerts and connected-appliance notifications are fairly familiar.
NFC tokens are a plausible, simple substitute for the panel, but tapping at the appliance doesn't really deliver mobility during cooking.
An IR thermopile with phone reporting lets users monitor from anywhere and replaces the window, though it isn't cheaper or simpler and the thermal mapping claim is a stretch.
A radical, wild robot microwave that comes to the user, but it is costly, unsafe with hot food, and the opposite of a simpler substitution.
A cordless battery-powered microwave is bold, but magnetron power draw makes it impractical, and carrying it doesn't remove the need to stand by it.
A disposable liner directly keeps the cavity clean and is plausible, though liners exist in other forms, and it adds waste and cost and risks arcing or fit issues.
Removes the roller-ring crevices, but magnetic levitation inside a microwave cavity is hard and costly, and it ignores the cavity walls.
A flush door is easier to wipe, but ITO shielding at 2.45 GHz with adequate attenuation and sealed edges is doubtful, and the mesh is a minor part of the cleaning burden.
Cavity airflow contributes little to dirt, since splatter comes from food, and heat pipes can't realistically replace the cooling at magnetron power levels.
Steam cleaning is feasible and effective but a common idea, and it substitutes a function rather than a part.
Removing the turntable helps cleaning somewhat, but the cavity walls still get splattered, and GaN phased arrays are costly, so the substitution is not cheaper or simpler.
A disposable film directly addresses splatter, but a film near food at heat raises fire and sag concerns, and it must cover the walls rather than only the ceiling.
Self-cleaning is highly relevant, but TiO2 with UV-A is slow and weak on baked grease, and it needs UV inside a microwave cavity.
This removes a minor crevice and bulb cover, but the lamp is not the main cleaning pain point, and a light pipe through a mesh door is questionable.
This is practical and cheap and makes the exterior easy to wipe, but it is common already and does not address the cavity interior.

Reflected-power load sensing is a genuinely clever substitution that auto-ends cooking, though inferring doneness from impedance is unreliable across varied foods and it mainly automates rather than gives feedback.
Gas sensing for doneness is plausible (some ovens already use humidity/gas sensors) and cheap, but it is more an addition than a substitution of the lamp and its signal is noisy.
Continuous rising-pitch audio gives real progress feedback and is simple to build, but it needs a temperature signal that it doesn't specify and could be annoying.
A wearable haptic alert is feasible and valuable for accessibility, but it adds parts rather than substituting cheaper ones and requires users to wear a band.
A thermopile eye gives real food temperature, but a germanium window is not cheap, and the sensor is unlikely to replace the magnetron thermal cutout safely since that is a separate safety function.
Solid-state RF is real and offers fine power control, but it is costly and a 50-150 W output may thaw slowly, so the gain for fast defrost is modest.
Solid-state phased-array field steering is plausible and improves uniformity, but it needs solid-state sources, so it is not a simple substitution.
Reflected-power sensing for automatic defrost is practical and helpful, though it adds sensing rather than substituting a part, and similar sensing already exists.
RF thawing at 27 MHz is proven in industry and heats thick blocks deeply, but it is hard to fit into a consumer unit and arcing is a risk.
A susceptor plate is feasible and cheap, but conductive heating from below is slow and uneven, so it helps little with fast defrosting.
Solid-state RF is real and plausible, and continuous power control does help defrosting, but it is expensive rather than a cheaper substitution and the thaw benefit is moderate.
Phase-steered multi-feed fields are real (solid-state RF cooking) and improve thaw uniformity, though they need solid-state sources and are not especially radical.
Sensing the thaw state through dielectric loss is sound in principle, but a floor pad is a weak coupling to food and it only stops the thaw rather than speeding it up.
This is a power-supply swap with little bearing on defrost speed, and it only makes sense alongside a solid-state RF source.
Ultrasonic heating of frozen food is a novel idea, but coupling air-to-food is poor and the heating is weak, so it is unlikely to speed thawing meaningfully.
A haptic ring alert directly frees the user to leave the kitchen and is easy to build, though wearable notifications for appliances are a known idea.
A rover that carries the ding to the user is wild and memorable and doable with existing robot parts, but it is costly and complex for a simple alert.
Smart-microwave app and voice control is common and mostly addresses starting rather than being notified, so it only partly serves mobility and is not radical.
A self-heating sleeve removes the appliance altogether and so fully removes standing by it, and it fits the substitute operator, though self-heating meals already exist.
A package NFC tag sets cook programs automatically and is plausible, but it reduces button-pressing more than it gives mobility during the cook.
Camera door is plausible and removes the mesh window, but the mesh is already a safe design, so the safety gain is modest.
Solid-state RF at 48 V removes the kV hazard directly; GaN microwave ovens exist, though cost and power level are still challenges.
Cool-touch exterior addresses a real burn risk; aerogel is plausible but costly, and it is not really cheaper or simpler as the operator requires.
mmWave presence sensing adds a redundant cutoff, but the interlock already covers the door and a radar inside a microwave cavity faces interference and heat.
Contactless power removes plug exposure, but kilowatt-level inductive transfer is inefficient and heating-prone, and the shock risk at a plug is already low.
A peel-out liner directly removes scrubbing, though a liner in the cavity risks fire, arcing and fit problems, and it adds recurring consumable cost.
Mode stirrers are proven in many real microwaves, so this is feasible and gives a flat floor, but the cleaning gain is modest and the cavity walls remain dirty.
A superhydrophobic coating plausibly eases cleaning, but durability against heat, grease and abrasion is doubtful, and baked-on splatter may still stick.
Pyrolysis at 250 C using the magnetron is implausible because empty-cavity magnetron operation damages it, and plastic parts and the door seal would not tolerate the heat.
Flush touch panels are common and easy to wipe, but they address only the exterior controls rather than the dirty interior.
Solid-state RF is real and offers control benefits, but magnetrons have negligible warm-up delay (about a second), so the speed claim is overstated and GaN cost is high.
IR sensing to end the cycle at a target temperature is plausible and useful, though already used in some ovens and it reads only surface temperature.
Phase-steered multi-feed heating needs solid-state RF sources, which makes it more expensive, but it addresses uneven heating and has real research behind it.
A drawer saves little time and needs good RF sealing, so it is feasible (drawer microwaves exist) but only marginally relevant to reheating speed.
A piezo voice alert is trivial and already common, and it does little to make reheating faster.
Solid-state RF is real and credible, with continuous power control and better even heating, though GaN cost at 700 W is high and the speed gain over a magnetron is modest.
NFC-driven heating profiles are plausible and give one-tap convenience, but they need packaging adoption and add components instead of substituting cheaper ones.
Mode stirrers are already standard in many microwaves, so this is feasible and useful for even heating but not radical, and it only indirectly speeds reheating.
Combination IR microwaves already exist, and browning does little for fast reheating, though the lamp substitution is simple.
A drawer microwave exists, but choke sealing and spill handling are harder, and it speeds loading only marginally.
Acoustic doneness detection works well for popcorn and plausibly for some foods, but it is not general and the microwave's own noise complicates it.
Humidity/VOC sensing in the vent is already used in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is feasible and relevant but not very radical.
A passive colour cue is a creative idea, but a liner measures cavity temperature rather than food temperature, and ink degradation and microwave heating are real problems.
The scent cue is original and reaches users who cannot hear the bell, but cartridge consumables, food-specificity and cost are problems.
Using the ITO door window as a dual-role capacitive sensor is very novel, but the Faraday shielding requirements and the noisy, harsh RF environment make it hard to realise.
Solid-state RF with phase steering is real and evens heating of milk, but it addresses breakfast-drink readiness only indirectly and the cost and power limits are significant.
Stirring milk to prevent superheating is relevant, but a magnet and stirrer bead inside a microwave cavity is hazardous (metal bead, arcing) and the turntable motor coupling is doubtful.
IR sensing of the liquid's surface temperature to stop at target directly delivers hot milk without guessing, and it is plausible, though surface-only readings and existing products limit novelty.
A thermochromic mug band is cheap and feasible and shows readiness, but it is a mug accessory rather than a lamp substitute and gives limited functional gain.
Hands-free door opening is convenient and plausible but barely touches the heating of milk, and it is a modest, incremental feature.
Practical and cheap substitution of the bell with a haptic BLE alert, but fairly obvious and not very radical.
Remote viewing helps monitoring without standing by, though it doesn't free the user from needing to attend at the end and cameras already exist in some ovens.
Remote control is feasible and well specified, but food still must be loaded and retrieved, and it's already common in smart ovens.
Wild and radical self-moving microwave directly answers mobility, but a heavy, hot appliance with mains power and spill/safety issues is impractical.
Truly radical portable heating pouch fits the need, but a compact shielded RF emitter drawing wireless power is hardly plausible for the power levels required.
Solid-state RF with continuous power is real technology and directly solves gentle butter melting, though it is costly and not really a cheaper or simpler substitute.
IR sensing to stop at butter's melt state fits the prep task well and is feasible, but sensor-based cooking is already known and the thermopile only reads the vessel surface.
A camera that judges doneness is plausible but serves baking monitoring more than prep, and microwave cakes rarely show browning.
A magnetic stir bar is clever and mixes while melting, but it is a hazard if the magnet couples poorly with the RF field, and the bar is stirred inside the batter.
A bottom drawer improves loading ergonomics but barely touches the butter-melting need, and RF sealing a drawer is difficult.
Solid-state RF with beam steering is real and promising for even heating, but the nutrient benefit is indirect and the cost is high; it is not really a cheaper substitute.
A tilted perforated rack is simple and feasible and drains fat, but it is a modest, fairly obvious change, and removing the turntable hurts evenness.
NIR doneness sensing is plausible and reduces overcooking, but food-surface readings are unreliable and the link to fat reduction is weak.
Susceptor sleeves already exist and work for oil-free crisping, so they are very feasible but not novel, and they are disposable packaging.
A vented steam-jacket liner is practical and strongly supports vitamin retention and oil-free cooking, though similar steam accessories exist.
Solid-state RF is real and gives precise temperature control for milk, though cost and the high-voltage-free claim make it a plausible but expensive substitute.
Directly serves the need with IR boil-detect, but it is an existing feature and not very radical.
Magnetic stirring addresses even heating and superheating well, but a ferrite stir-bar inside a microwave raises arcing and metal-in-cavity concerns, and it needs special cups.
A single-mug cavity suits breakfast drinks, but single-mode cavities are sensitive to load and the claim of no hot spots is optimistic.
A patch antenna feed cuts parts, but its link to hot milk is indirect and power handling and spatter exposure are real problems.

Stirring to prevent superheating is clever and relevant, but a magnetic stir bar in a microwave cavity is hard (the magnets and stir plate must survive the RF field, and the PTFE bar is awkward); the idea also ignores that the turntable's real job is even heating.
IR temperature-based shutoff directly delivers a perfectly hot drink and is quite plausible, though not very radical and surface reading can mislead.
Passive colour cue is cheap and simple, but the door glass temperature poorly represents milk temperature and the lamp has other uses.
Inverter-like continuous power control is feasible and helps gentle warming, but it's an existing technology and not radical; the triac/transformer description is also somewhat muddled.
A multisensory ready cue is charming and fits the breakfast ritual, but it only addresses the alert, not heating the drink; aroma cartridge adds cost.
Saves only a small lamp load (LED lamps are already tiny), and ambient light through a dark door mesh would give poor visibility, so the benefit is marginal.
Solid-state RF is a real, emerging technology that improves efficiency and control, but cost and power level remain hurdles, and it is not really a cheaper or simpler substitute.
Sensor-based auto-cook already exists in commercial microwaves, but it does cut wasted energy, and it is practical to build.
Thermoelectric recovery yields very little power, and removing the fan risks magnetron overheating, so the energy gain is doubtful.
Phased-array steering is plausible with solid-state RF and improves heating uniformity, but the motor saving is tiny and the added feeds increase complexity.
An IR sensor that stops heating at the melt point directly solves butter melting and is plausible, though IR sensing in microwaves already exists and surface readings can mislead.
Induction in a cavity floor is a radical swap that works for metal bowls, but it removes the microwave function and conflicts with the product's nature, with limited cake-baking value.
A magnetically driven stirrer is plausible and addresses hot spots and scorching, but a PTFE paddle in a microwave raises complications and it is not much cheaper than a turntable.
A low-voltage graphene heater is wild and safe-sounding, but it is a hot plate rather than a microwave, and cavity-floor heating would be slow and would not bake a cake.
A thermochromic window gives passive melt feedback cheaply, but a door window sits at a different temperature than the butter, so it is an unreliable indicator and only mildly radical.
Auto-doneness sensing directly saves time and guesswork; sensor fusion is plausible but accuracy through steam and varied foods is hard, and similar features already exist in premium ovens.
Solid-state RF is real and offers instant, precise power, but cost is high and the time-saving link is indirect (the 'cheaper' substitute criterion is not met yet).
Electronic beam steering would give even heating without stirring, saving effort, but it needs solid-state arrays and is complex in a closed cavity.
Simple, cheap and feasible, and frees the user to leave the kitchen, though it is an incremental idea and not radical.
A gesture-opened drawer is novel and convenient but saves little cooking time, and sealing and cost are challenging.
