Solid-state RF is real and gives gentle control, but it is a known direction and costs more rather than simplifying, so it is only a loose fit with the substitute operator.
NFC tap recipes are very feasible and convenient, but they only ease the interface and do little for milk heating quality.
A ceramic nucleation rod is a cheap, simple substitute that addresses superheating, though porous ceramic is hard to clean and milk can foul it.
A single-mug coaxial applicator is a radical redesign with plausible even heating, but it is hard to engineer safely and to load and unload mugs.
Thermal camera to watch butter melt is useful and concrete, though LWIR through a mesh window is hard (mesh blocks LWIR) and it isn't really a cheaper substitution.
Reflected-power sensing to detect melt endpoint directly addresses butter melting without guesswork, though small loads give weak signals and it adds components rather than substituting.
Solid-state phased array for independent bowl heating is radical and relevant to multi-step prep, but costly and hard to achieve selective heating in a small cavity.
Susceptor browning is plausible and well-known tech, but it targets baking the cake rather than prep tasks like melting butter.
Easy and practical for messy hands, but only tangentially tied to melting or baking prep and not very radical.
Weight-to-time is plausible and removes settings, but weight poorly predicts needed heating for varied foods, and the load cell adds cost rather than simplifying.
Tap-to-cook is effortless for tagged meals, but it depends on packaging adoption and fails for untagged food, and NFC is not a cheaper substitute.
The door-ajar cue is a clever, intuitive end signal, but it only addresses opening and finishing, not setting the cook.
One button with stop-when-hot is the most direct path to zero learning, though IR only reads surface temperature and the sensor is not cheaper.
The dish acting as the control is a quirky, mechanically simple substitution, but the program per shape is crude and ignores food type.
Reflected-power sensing is plausible and cuts overcooking waste, though it is somewhat known and doneness correlation is imperfect; it also doesn't clearly substitute a part.
Solid-state RF is real and efficiency gains are plausible, but GaN cost and power levels are challenging, and magnetrons are already fairly efficient.
Phased feeds can steer fields and remove the turntable, but the turntable motor uses negligible energy so the gain is small and multiple RF sources are costly.
Feasible and simple, but real microwave lamps are ~15-25 W of minor total energy and LED would be the more obvious substitute; camera adds cost.
Passive cooling and heat recovery is creative, but a magnetron needs substantial cooling, TEG yield is tiny, and fan removal is risky.
A low-res IR camera gives continuous, direct doneness feedback and is plausible, though it is a bit pricey and the 'substitute cheaper' angle is weak; the IR window must be handled in the cavity.
Using the cabinet as a contact microphone is clever and tied to how people judge doneness, but magnetron noise and fan noise make robust detection hard.
Passive and cheap, but a turntable coating only senses the plate's temperature, which is unreliable for food doneness, and the dye must survive repeated heating and washing.
Core temperature is the ideal signal, but a battery-free RFID tag with a metal tine inside a microwave cavity risks arcing and field interference, so it is hard to make work.
A scent-based ready signal is radical and works from another room, but VOC sensing of doneness is noisy, and a consumable cartridge adds cost and the scent may be unwelcome.
Microwave lamps are typically ~20-25 W but only on during cooking, so savings are small; ambient light through a door fibre pipe would be too dim to see food well.
IR sensor cutoff is real and avoids overheating, but sensor cooking already exists and surface-only readings limit its accuracy.
Inverter microwaves are already commercial and do improve power control, though the efficiency gains are modest and the idea is not radical.
Solid-state multi-feed phase steering is real and removes the motor, but the motor's draw is tiny and solid-state RF sources are costly.
Thermoelectric recovery is creative, but at ~5% conversion efficiency it yields milliwatts at best and does not touch the main energy loss.
Solid-state GaN RF replacing the magnetron is real and enables fine power control, but the nutrient benefit is indirect and the cost is high.
Steam cooking directly serves nutrient retention and fat-free cooking and is very feasible, though steam-assist microwaves already exist.
A thermal camera to prevent overcooking is plausible and useful, but the link to nutrients is indirect and metal-mesh doors complicate IR viewing.
Passive heat-pipe waste heat for steam is clever, but magnetron heat is low-grade and modest, so generating meaningful steam is doubtful.
Susceptor browning is proven and cuts oil, though it is an existing concept and does nothing for nutrient retention.
Replacing the lamp with a camera is plausible and saves some power, but the lamp is a minor share of total energy and a camera phone link adds standby load.
Sensor cooking already exists in commercial microwaves but does cut wasted run-time, so it is relevant and feasible, though not radical.
Solid-state RF with beamforming is a real, researched direction that improves efficiency and control, though cost and power levels remain challenges.
Heat recovery is conceptually relevant, but the magnetron's waste heat is low-grade, the household use is odd, and the heat-pipe cooling must be reliable enough to replace the fan.
An electropermanent latch is workable and cuts holding power, but the savings are tiny relative to cooking energy.
GaN solid-state RF removes the lethal HV capacitor hazard and is a real technology, though cost and 1 kW power at 48 V remain challenges.
Phased-array steering is real and removes the turntable, but its link to safety is indirect and mostly about even heating.

Dual-channel monitored interlock with leakage sensing directly targets radiation exposure, though capacitive sensing in the door gap and real-time leakage detection are tricky and the failure modes are not fully eliminated.
Aerogel insulation to keep the cabinet cool addresses burns well, but cost is high and the shift from a steel wrapper is questionable, since the metal enclosure also serves as RF shielding.
Removing the window and lamp cuts a leak path and a hot bulb, but users dislike the lack of visibility and the mesh window is already well shielded.
Sensing doneness removes timing effort and overcook or recook cycles, and similar sensor-based cooking exists, though gas sensing in a hot steamy cavity is hard.
Solid-state RF is real and removes the turntable and the stirring step, but it saves only modest time and the unit is costly rather than a simple substitution.
Plausible and cheap, but it depends on packaging adoption, and the time saved is only a few seconds of button pressing.
A gimmicky mechanism that saves a couple of seconds at most while adding cost and a reliability risk, and the cooking time is unchanged.
It directly cuts heating time and is a bold substitution, but a heat battery for food needs high temperatures, contact transfer and safety work, and it is no longer a microwave.
Reflected-power doneness sensing is a plausible, concrete way to end timer guessing, though reflection changes are subtle and a hard-to-calibrate proxy for doneness.
Solid-state RF with phase control already exists in products and prototypes, so it is credible, but the time savings come mainly from even heating and are modest.
A package NFC tag that sets the program is simple and feasible, but similar barcode and RFID ideas already exist, and it needs industry adoption.
A continuous tunnel oven with choke ports is a real industrial concept and is radical for home use, but it is bulky and a poor fit for household needs.
Ultrasonic thawing is intriguing, but coupling acoustic energy into food in air is poor, and a piezo plate can't be combined with RF cooking so simply.
Highly practical and directly frees the user to leave, but a wearable alert is an incremental, fairly obvious idea and a weak fit for the radical brief.
A self-driving tray that delivers the meal is wild and on-need, but it faces a microwave-safe electronics problem and hot-food spill risks.
An open-top resonant heating mat with a receiver dish is radical and lets the user walk away, though it is hard to do efficiently and safely, and it shifts away from microwaves.
Auto-stop doneness sensing reduces the need to attend, but the user still has to be nearby at the end or collect the food, so it serves mobility only partly.
A flying heated food pod is very wild but impractical, unsafe indoors and thermally inefficient, and it is hardly a simpler substitute.
Zero-interaction cooking for packaged food is highly relevant, though it needs industry-wide tag adoption and does nothing for non-packaged food.
A clever physical done-signal, but it only addresses the end of the cycle and not the setup that creates the learning curve.
Closed-loop temperature control removes power-level decisions, but the user still has to set a target or time and IR surface sensing is limited.
Removing the turntable simplifies placement, but solid-state phase-steered RF is costly and not a cheaper substitute, and operation itself is unchanged.
A very simple, buildable tap-to-add interface that is intuitive, though it resembles existing quick-start buttons.
Solid-state RF is real and efficiency gains are plausible (better control, no filament warm-up), though GaN cost is high and the substitution is not cheaper; it is well known in the industry.
Matching cavity to load is a sensible efficiency idea, but a motorized resonant telescoping cavity is mechanically complex, and it is hard to keep it matched at 2.45 GHz and to seal against leakage.
Thermoelectric harvesting recovers only a few percent of the waste heat, so the net gain is tiny. Removing the fan likely risks overheating, and the idea adds cost instead of simplifying.
Sensor-based auto-stop already exists in commercial microwaves and clearly cuts overcooking waste, but it is an incremental idea and only loosely a substitution.
Insulation helps little in a microwave because the cavity walls are not heated and cooking is brief, and a vacuum panel near the RF cavity is awkward; keep-warm via stored heat is weakly justified.
Probe-guided closed-loop thermal control is plausible and helps nutrient retention, though microwave heating is uneven and the probe itself is a known concept.
A sloped, perforated fat-drain rack is simple and workable, but it is an incremental, familiar idea and only reduces fat modestly.
Ending the cook on a modelled cumulative nutrient-loss threshold is novel, but it needs core temperature data and food-specific kinetics that are hard to get in practice.
An ultrasonic steam cavity serves fat reduction and vitamin retention well and is feasible, though steam-microwave combos already exist.
Live NIR fat readouts are eye-catching, but they only inform the user rather than change the cooking, and in-cavity NIR sensing is hard to do.
Solid-state RF is real and gives gentle, precise power control, but the nutrient benefit over the existing inverter is modest and indirect.
Steam injection directly reduces fat and nutrient leaching and is feasible, but steam-assist ovens already exist.
A fat-draining rack is simple and feasible and cuts fat directly, but it is a well-known, incremental accessory.
NIR doneness sensing is plausible and avoids overcooking, but it is hard to make accurate inside a microwave cavity and the nutrient link is indirect.
A pressure-sealed RF-transparent ceramic lid would cut cook time and nutrient loss, but pressure safety and certification make it hard and risky.
NFC-read packaging removes all settings and is plausible, though it only works for tagged food and requires industry adoption.
A progress halo is intuitive, but it only shows status and does not simplify input or operation.
Solid-state RF steering is a genuinely radical substitution, but it is costly and only indirectly helps ease of use.
Easy and cheap push-to-open, but a modest improvement over existing door handles and buttons.
Steam-sensing auto-stop removes timer guesswork, but sensor-based cooking already exists in many microwaves.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and eliminates kilovolt shock at the source, though not very novel and still costly.
A transparent ferrofluid window is wildly novel, but ferrofluids are opaque and the physics and sealing are implausible.
Removes a minor burn source, but a cavity coating would not glow bright enough for viewing, and the microwave bulb isn't a major hazard.
Solid-state phased arrays can steer fields and remove the turntable, though the safety gain is modest.
IR sensing with automatic cutoff plausibly reduces overheating and burns, but it is an incremental, existing concept and does not address radiation or shock.
Directly solves butter melt endpoint, plausible with IR thermopile, though surface-only reading and IR sensing in microwaves already exist.
Inverter microwaves already exist (Panasonic), so it is a real fix for gentle melting but not very radical.
Stirring paddle in place of turntable is a clever, simple substitution for even melting, though sealing, bowl fit and cleaning are challenges.
Susceptor base is workable and adds browning for cake, but the link to butter melting and a birthday cake is partial.
Feasible and convenient but a peripheral notification gadget that doesn't change the heating or baking function.
Using reflected RF power as a doneness signal is clever and reuses existing hardware, though mapping reflection to doneness reliably across foods is hard.
Acoustic boil/sizzle detection is plausible and already partly seen in commercial products, but it only works for foods that make distinct sounds.
A glanceable color-changing cabinet is striking, but heat-piping cavity heat to the outer skin is impractical and a hot outer surface is a safety concern.
Thermopile array imaging gives direct, spatial temperature feedback and is feasible, though not highly radical and a microwave-opaque IR window needs care.
A scent cue is a fresh sensory channel that works with the door closed, but it is a consumable that is imprecise and could be annoying or unreliable.
Spoken food-state feedback addresses a real blindness gap, though a camera in a microwave cavity faces heat, steam and splatter, and bone-conduction speaker makes little sense in an appliance.
Detented tactile timer with vibration alert is highly practical and directly helps low-vision users, but is a fairly incremental idea.
Single start bar with automatic power reduces cognitive load, though sensor-based cooking already exists and reliability is variable.
A big pull bar is easy to find and operate, simple and feasible, but quite obvious and already seen on some ovens.
Fixed dish with mode stirrer is a real, feasible substitution that aids locating food, though it leaves other accessibility problems and is not wildly novel.
Mode stirrers are an existing technique in many ovens, so it is plausible and cheaper but not radical, and it improves uniformity rather than thaw speed.
Reflected-power end-point sensing is plausible and directly serves thaw control, though the signal is noisy and the idea is not new in principle.
Inverter microwaves already exist and give true low-power thaw, so this is highly feasible and relevant but hardly novel.
A PCM pack cannot dump magnetron heat for long runs and is likely to saturate, so it barely serves defrost speed.
An NFC package thaw profile is creative and convenient, but it needs ecosystem adoption and does not speed up thawing itself.
Gas sensing of exhaust volatiles for doneness is plausible and directly answers the need, though it is similar to existing sensor-cook ideas and the sensor would need to be calibrated per food.
Acoustic doneness detection is plausible and relevant, but the microphone must survive heat and fan noise, and the sounds only reflect part of doneness.

A passive heat map is creative, but thermochromic film inside a microwave is a problem: it only shows surface temperature, the film is hard to place and keep intact, and it would not let anyone see the food once it goes dark.

A progress skin that doubles as the RF shield is very radical and gives a glanceable indicator, but a conductive polymer cannot shield microwaves as well as metal and the idea is impractical as described.
Load cells under the turntable are feasible and measure a real physical signal, but mass loss is an indirect proxy for doneness and gives no feedback for many foods.
Steam-sensing auto-stop directly removes time and power settings, and some microwaves already offer sensor cooking, so it is plausible but not very radical.
Solid-state beam steering is a real technique and replaces the turntable, but it only removes a minor placement rule and does little for operating simplicity.
A spring-ajar door as the done signal is a clever, cheap mechanical substitution, but it only covers the completion cue and not operation.
An LED status halo is easy to build and readable at a glance, but it is a modest idea that does not simplify the controls.
Tagged plates that load their own program remove the need to choose settings, though NFC tags near RF and metal and the need for special plates are practical problems.
Spoken status helps low-vision users, but sensing cooking state is hard and it doesn't truly substitute the lamp; it's partly a talking-microwave variant.
NFC tap-to-cook with tactile tags directly removes dial reading and fine motor needs, though it depends on packaging tag adoption.
Detented tray stop positions are plausible and help locate food, but it's a modest benefit and the description is thin and slightly contradictory.
A waist-height drawer microwave exists in commercial form and helps mobility, but RF sealing and heat-rated slides are challenging and it addresses vision less.
A BLE wrist haptic alert is feasible and valuable for deaf-blind users, though it's an add-on wearable and only covers one aspect of use.
Solid-state RF is real and already commercialized with better control, but it is not inherently faster at thawing and GaN at these powers is costly, so it is not truly a cheaper substitute.
RF thawing at 27 MHz is proven in industry and genuinely speeds up thawing of large blocks, but runaway heating and arcing with uneven loads make a consumer version difficult.
Detecting the ice-to-water transition is a smart end point, but it helps accuracy more than speed, and the piezo chime part is a loosely related add-on.
Susceptor plates are feasible, but they heat the food by conduction and will likely cook the surface rather than speed up an even thaw.
Waste heat from the magnetron is small and at low temperature, so pre-thawing would be slow and weak, and the extra drawer adds cost.
A tap replaces dials and is highly accessible, but it needs tagged packaging, which limits it, and NFC food tags are not a wholly new idea.
Spoken doneness cues help blind users, but classifying sounds inside a noisy, hot, microwave-filled cavity is hard and the microphone must survive that environment.
A ridged tray is cheap and easy to make but only modestly helps, and it may make cleaning and plate stability worse.
A sliding door with a tactile rail is plausible, but magnetic latching raises microwave-safety interlock concerns and a vertical door may be awkward for hot dishes.

A thermal braille map is very novel and conveys useful information, but placing SMA dots on a door that is hot and sits next to a microwave field is hard, and the thermopile must see through the cavity.
Thermochromic door is a charming visual cue, but the dye would respond to door temperature rather than butter temperature, and it removes the lamp, which makes viewing harder.
IR target-temperature stop directly solves the butter-melting precision problem and is feasible with existing thermopile arrays.
A PTC conductive melt dish is inventive and suits gentle melting, but it departs from microwave heating and the low-voltage winding adds complexity.
Solid-state RF gives fine power control ideal for melting and tempering; it is real technology but costly, and it is not a cheaper substitute.
A hands-free door is practical for messy hands but only peripherally supports the baking and melting task.
A bimetal thermostat melt-stop is plausible and directly serves butter melting, but it is a simple, familiar mechanism, and sensing the bowl's temperature through a disc is questionable.
A magnetic stir bar driven by the turntable motor is clever and concrete, though a metal-free bar and magnet ring near the magnetron raise some practical concerns.
An IR camera on the door is novel and specific, but it is costly and complicated, runs against the 'cheaper or simpler' substitute brief, and has to cope with the metal mesh and steam.
A thermochromic doneness probe is simple and useful for cake baking, but permanent color-change pigments that are food-safe and microwave-compatible need work, and it targets baking rather than prep.
Proofing is only loosely relevant to a birthday cake, which is usually not yeast-leavened, and gasket-based humid holding is an incremental idea.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and removes the 2 kV rail, though it doesn't eliminate leakage risk since RF is still generated and cost is high.
Radar presence sensing is plausible and adds protection, but it replaces the mechanical interlock, which is a safety regression since redundancy is required, and food motion causes false positives.
Beam steering removes the glass plate and is tied to solid-state RF, but the safety gain is modest and it needs a complex array.
Aerogel insulation is feasible and cuts exterior burns, but it is a fairly obvious thermal fix, a minor hazard in microwaves, and expensive.
ITO-coated panels and LED lighting are plausible, but the mesh is already effective for shielding, so the leakage gain is marginal and ITO durability and attenuation are concerns.
VOC sensing of doneness is plausible (some ovens have humidity sensors), but aroma-based doneness is noisy across foods and the sensor drifts.
Listening for sizzle is creative, but microwave fan noise, the lack of a Maillard-type sizzle in most microwaved food, and the harsh cavity make it unreliable.
Reflected-power sensing reuses existing hardware and is physically grounded, though it is hard to map to doneness for varied foods.
A load cell is simple and feasible, and mass loss correlates with dryness, but it is a weak doneness proxy and the turntable's rotation complicates the mount.
Passive thermochromic feedback is cheap and simple, but cavity air temperature does not reflect food readiness, and the film must survive the door's mesh and heat conditions.
Spoken doneness feedback directly serves visually impaired users, but gas sensors reliably inferring food state is questionable and it adds parts rather than substituting simpler ones.
Raising the plate helps mobility-limited users, but it addresses reach rather than vision, and a motorised lift inside a microwave cavity is hard (RF, spills, load) and not cheaper.
A big touch target helps arthritis and tremor, but a flat touch surface gives no tactile cue for blind users and risks accidental door opening.
The haptic wristband is feasible and helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users, but it is an add-on accessory that does not substitute any part and does little for vision.
Tactile braille cards replace knobs with a readable control and the substitution is clear, though lost cards and the limited program set are drawbacks.
Practical and plausible, but it only protects the waveguide cover, a minor cleaning pain point, and similar splatter covers already exist.
Highly feasible and already common on modern microwaves, so it is not radical, and it addresses the exterior panel rather than the interior.
Wildly novel and removes the tray, but acoustic levitation cannot hold typical food portions or hot liquids and would interact badly with microwaves.
Photocatalytic self-cleaning walls are a clever and concrete idea, but UV-A TiO2 breakdown of baked-on grease is slow and weak at this scale, and it would need to cope with microwave fields.
A steam-clean cycle using the magnetron is practical and directly aids cleaning, but steam-cleaning bowls and similar features are well known.
Practical and cheap substitution of bell with a wrist haptic, directly frees the user from earshot but is a fairly obvious idea.
Passively prevents superheating so walking away is safer, though it only addresses liquids and dispensing grit in food is questionable.
Remote control plus camera strongly serves mobility and is concrete, but it is already existing in smart ovens and not radical, nor really a cheaper substitute.
Truly radical and wild, a mobile oven that comes to the user, though costly, hot-liquid hazards and impractical for homes.
Improves safety for unattended use but only indirectly serves mobility and is mostly a component swap.
Catalytic liners exist in ovens, but they work at about 200°C+ while microwave walls stay cool, so passive self-cleaning is unlikely to work.
A gasket-free door is a cleaner surface, but ITO shielding at microwave leakage levels and with no choke seal is doubtful and safety-critical.
Flat touch panels are already common and easy to wipe, but they only address the exterior controls, not the main cleaning burden.
Mode stirrers with a fixed plate already exist in flatbed microwaves, and this removes a real crumb trap and makes the plate easier to clean.
A sacrificial film roll is a radical idea that does address cleaning, but it adds consumables, and heat, arcing and food-contact problems make it hard to build.
IR and humidity sensing for auto-stop is plausible and removes timer guesswork, though it saves little actual heating time and sensor fouling by steam is a risk.
NFC-tagged packaging is technically easy and cuts setup to one gesture, but it depends on food makers adopting the tags and a metal cavity complicates reader placement.
Solid-state phased-array heating without a turntable is radical and does improve uniformity, but it is costly and not simpler or cheaper, so it strays from the substitute brief.
A motorised tray is feasible but adds complexity and saves only seconds, so it barely serves fast reheating.
A supercapacitor buffer for burst power directly shortens heating time and is imaginative, but a 1500 W magnetron burst is limited by the 13 A socket, by cost, and by recharge time between uses.
Closing the door to start is intuitive and simple, though the default cycle may over- or under-heat varied foods and the self-opening door is a gimmick.
Tagged dishes remove power selection, but they need special cookware and NFC tags near microwave fields, which makes this a niche ecosystem.
Steam-based doneness detection exists in some ovens and removes timer setting, while the aroma cartridge adds a quirky but consumable-dependent signal.
Natural-language control eliminates the learning curve, but voice is a well-known approach and is less of a cheaper or simpler substitution.
A progress ring is easy to read, but it only displays status and does not simplify starting or setting the cook.
Humidity-based auto-stop exists in sensor-cook microwaves, but it is cheap, practical and saves time and guesswork.
Acoustic doneness sensing is fresh and could cut door-peeking, but the noisy cavity and varied foods make classification unreliable, and the time saving is modest.
Solid-state RF arrays are real and already in prototypes, and they remove the turntable, but they are costly and the time saved comes only from avoiding reheats.
Easy to build, but it saves only a second or two and may be a nuisance or safety issue with hot food.
Auto-cook presets with weight sensing are well established, and the gain is mostly convenience rather than a large time saving.
Load-cell weighing is already used in some commercial microwaves, so it is practical and well-targeted at defrost but not radical.
Solid-state RF replacing the magnetron is real and gives better control, but it is costly and the gain over inverter microwaves is modest for defrosting.
27 MHz RF tempering is proven industrially for thawing blocks and addresses the need directly, though it is hard to miniaturize for the home and the uneven heating risk (runaway) remains.
A thermopile IR array is plausible and helps endpoint detection, but it sees only the surface and does not speed up thawing.
A susceptor plate adds bottom heating, but thawing speed gains are limited and cracking or overheating is a real risk.
Solid-state RF with continuous power modulation is real and gently cooks with better nutrient retention, though it replaces the magnetron with a costlier part rather than a cheaper one.
Returning condensate is plausible and novel, but the vitamin loss through steam is small and a closed loop in a microwave cavity is awkward.

A SiC susceptor lid that browns without oil directly cuts added fat, and susceptor technology is proven, though it is an incremental refinement.
IR thermopile sensing of milk temperature directly serves the hot-drink need and is very practical, though IR sensing in microwaves is not radical.

A magnetic stirrer under the cup adds froth, but it is a metal stirrer inside a microwave, which is problematic and adds a function more than it substitutes.

Thermochromic mugs already exist and are cheap, but they only indicate temperature and do not heat the milk, and the 'replaces the bell' claim is weak.
Magnetic stirring gives even heating and prevents skin, but a metallic or magnet-bearing stir bead in a microwave cavity risks arcing and the turntable removal is doubtful.

Replacing the magnetron with induction is radical and workable as a cooktop, but it is no longer a microwave and needs special jugs, so it only loosely serves the brief.
Plausible and convenient, but it depends on packaging adoption and is not really a cheaper substitution of the knobs.

Feasible and handy, but it barely affects reheating speed and the accidental-opening risk is real.

Removing the hot lamp is a small safety gain, since microwave lamps are low-heat, and persistent phosphor glow fades and may be too dim, but the substitution is clever and simple.

A load-cell turntable gives a real progress signal, but mass loss is an imperfect proxy and the load cell must work inside a microwave cavity.

Easy to build and useful for multitasking, but it is an obvious idea that does not shorten cooking time.

Whimsical and radical, but it only addresses end-of-cycle and still leaves the user to set the cooking; the lift mechanism adds cost and risk (hot food, spills).

A disposable sleeve makes cleaning easy, but it creates waste, risks fit and fire problems, and covers like microwave lids already exist.
Targets the real stored-charge shock hazard, but a magnetron needs ~4kV and a capped-energy supply delivering kW of power is hard; the claim is plausible only partly.
Real-time leakage sensing with cutoff directly addresses radiation safety and is plausible, though replacing the choke with a sensor loop is questionable since the choke still must contain RF.
Cool-touch glass and LED lighting reduce burn risk modestly, and ITO as RF shield is plausible but conductive coatings are lossy and leakage-prone; burn hazard is mainly from food.
Sensor-driven boil-over stop prevents scald injuries and is feasible with humidity/IR sensors, though similar sensor cooking exists already.
Cordless inductive power removes the exposed cord, but transferring kW wirelessly is inefficient and the pedestal still holds mains, so shock is shifted rather than removed.
